entry.content:
1 minute read
Pro Tools 2026.11: Extensions, Stem Separator, MPE
2:29

Avid has released Pro Tools 2026.11, adding a third-party Extensions format and an AI Stem Separator. MPE support and Windows High DPI scaling also arrive.

Avid has released Pro Tools 2026.11, which adds a new plugin format called Pro Tools Extensions, an AI-powered Stem Separator, MIDI Polyphonic Expression (MPE), and Windows improvements.

Extensions add third-party tools

Unlike traditional AAX plugins, which operate on individual tracks, Extensions can support processes spanning multiple tracks or entire sessions. They are accessed from the Pro Tools Edit window. Partners at launch include Pro Sound Effects and Soundly (sound effects libraries), Forte (track importing, organization, and delivery), and Pibox (collaboration and feedback). The existing Splice and SoundFlow integrations from 2025 will also be available as Extensions, including their AI-enabled capabilities.

AI Stem Separator

The Pro Tools Stem Separator Extension separates recordings into up to six stems: vocals, drums, bass, guitar, keys, and other. It works without exporting files to external applications or uploading audio to cloud services. Users drag audio into the Extension, preview the stems, and bring them back into the session as individual tracks. It is included at no additional cost with all versions of Pro Tools, including the free Pro Tools Intro.

MPE and Windows updates

MPE lets individual notes respond independently to gestures such as pressure and pitch movement, whereas in conventional MIDI changes like pitch bend typically affect multiple notes at once. It requires compatible controllers and virtual instruments, and also allows real-time manipulation of timbre, filters, and effects.

On Windows, the release adds High DPI support for 2K, 4K, and 8K monitors, per-monitor scaling, enhanced compatibility scaling, and improved dark theme support for title bars, menus, and common dialogs. Playlist Clip Color Coding gives consistent colors across tracks for different takes.

Availability and upgrades

Pro Tools 2026.11 is available now to Pro Tools Artist, Studio, and Ultimate subscribers, perpetual license holders with an active upgrade plan, and Pro Tools Intro users. All major new enhancements are supported across Pro Tools versions, including the 30-day trial. More information is at www.avid.com/pro-tools.

entry.content:
2 minute read
iZotope Photon: GPU stem separation, price, specs
2:52

iZotope's Photon uses multiple models on your GPU to split stems and clean up noisy audio. It's available now as a standalone app and ARA plugin.

iZotope has launched Photon, a standalone app and ARA plugin for AI-powered stem separation and audio enhancement that uses 12 custom-trained models and runs locally on the GPU, with no uploads. Perhaps more significantly than that, for the long term at least, Photon is the first collaboration between the iZotope and Boris FX research teams.

It can split music into four stems, separate drums into individual elements [Handy for trying to work out what on earth Danny Carey is up to this time. Drumming Ed], isolate vocals, identify and separate speakers, and clean up noisy recordings. As an ARA plugin, it lets users run several models together and switch between them. Previews can start at any point in a clip. Model Manager downloads new and updated models without a reinstall.

Demix

  • Music 4 Stems: 4-stem separation model for music.
  • Music 4 Stems Ultra: new 4-stem separation model for music.
  • Drums 5 Stems: kick, snare, hi-hat, toms, and cymbals.
  • Voice Separator: splits up to 6 speakers from one audio file into individual stems.
  • Voice 2 Stems: voice and music.
  • Cinema 4 Stems: splits a video or audio file into dialogue, music, sound effects, and everything else.

Denoise

  • Voice Restore: handles speech, noise, levels, mic tone, and reverb.
  • Indoor / Indoor Noisy: reverb and room noise.
  • Outdoor / Outdoor Traffic / Outdoor Wind: models for traffic, urban noise, and heavy wind.

Formats and exports

Exports are WAV, FLAC, MP3, or video in the same format as the source, with the original video stream kept. Photon opens a lot too, namely .wav, .mp3, .flac, .aiff, .aif, .aac, .m4a, .mp4, .mkv, .mov, .mxf, and .mpg files. For video, it reads the audio track and can write the processed audio back.

Photon price and availability

Photon is available now at izotope.com/products/photon, with cyber deals through December 7, 2026. Prices are MSRP, with cyber prices in brackets.

  • Photon: $349 ($259)
  • Crossgrade from any paid iZotope product: $269 ($179)
  • Crossgrade from RX Elements (or any bundle that includes it): $199 ($129)
  • Crossgrade from RX Standard (or any bundle that includes it): $149 ($74)
  • Crossgrade from RX Advanced (or any bundle that includes it): $99 ($49)
  • Subscription: $19/month ($12 first month, then $19/month) or $119/year ($89 first year, then $119/year)

Photon requires macOS 14 or later on Apple silicon (Intel Macs are not supported), or Windows 10 or later, 64-bit, with a GPU of at least 4 GB VRAM. 16 GB of RAM is recommended and 8 GB is the minimum.

DaVinci Resolve 21.2: new features and fixes
7:20

DaVinci Resolve 21.2 supports MacBook Pro PROLED XDR touch screens and Gen 6 LUTs. Studio adds AI assistant tools, while Fusion Studio and Fairlight Live also update.

Blackmagic Design's dev team has been hard at work as usual, and DaVinci Resolve 21.2 was uploaded to its servers overnight.

Because the company often works closely with Apple, this software update adds support for Apple MacBook Pro laptops with PROLED XDR displays as well as up to 5x faster rendering for M5 Pro and M5 Max Apple silicon chips. This update also adds support for Blackmagic Generation 6 Color Science LUTs and film looks (we covered the Gen 6 release here), as well as source timecode for extracted audio files. There are also fixes for network drive audio issues with some MXF clips and for AAF audio timecode accuracy from interlaced media, plus OGraf template loading and render fixes.

The paid DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2 version, which is still 20% off at $236 until November 20, adds a few further tweaks, mainly in the AI assistant area. You can find the full list of its additional features below.

Fusion Studio 21.2 adds OGraf and Text+ fixes

Fusion Studio 21.2 has also been updated. Blackmagic says it improves stability, with fixes for custom tool control naming, Text+ CLS border extension anchoring, and OGraf template loading and rendering. The OGraf inspector now shows up to 35 template properties.

Fairlight Live 1.1.1 supports two new control panels

And finally, the new Fairlight Live 1.1.1 release adds support for Fairlight Live Audio Panel 20 and Fairlight Live Audio Panel 40. Blackmagic's control surfaces now cover 10, 20, and 40 faders supported by 1, 2, and 4 touchscreens, and provide controls for layers, bus, matrix, aux, VCA, sub-masters, talkback, and more. Prices scale from $2415 to $8245.

The latest software also includes templates for new ATEM Constellation IP switchers, improves audio I/O management and error reporting, and adds user-defined screen mapping and a panel screensaver after a period of inactivity.

All downloads are free and available from the Blackmagic Design Support Center.

Full release notes for each package

Here's the full list of new features and fixes per package.

What's new in DaVinci Resolve 21.2

The following features have been added or updated.

  • Support for Apple MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR touch screens.
  • Support for Blackmagic Design Gen 6 LUTs.
  • Extracted audio files now retain source timecode.
  • Multicam clips now open as source clips in source timelines.
  • Open in Timeline with Source Viewer supports clips and multicams.
  • Menu action and shortcut to restore last active edit points.
  • Command or Ctrl marquee selection now uses last edit point type.
  • Conform lock multiple timeline clips to one media pool clip.
  • Convert in out to compound clip replaces clips in situ.
  • Separate context action to create compound clip from in out range.
  • Stop playback option applies to playhead nudges and mouse clicks.
  • Edit menu options now persist after UI layout reset.
  • Support for EXIF metadata in PNG files.
  • Addressed network drive audio issues for some MXF clips.
  • Addressed slow MP3 audio only renders.
  • Addressed missing clips in some AAF imports.
  • Addressed incorrect audio timecode for AAF with interlaced media.
  • Addressed OGraf template loading from network and zipped paths.
  • Addressed OGraf render timeouts and memory usage issues.
  • Addressed slow loading of media from XDCAM drives.
  • Addressed flashing media offline frames with some H.265 clips.
  • Addressed source track changes in collaboration source timelines.
  • Addressed hang editing MultiText keyframes during render cache.
  • Addressed issues with italics in imported TTML subtitles.
  • Addressed data burn scaling issues for render resolutions.
  • Addressed HE-AAC decode issues for some clips on Windows.
  • Addressed incorrect channel order for WAV files with iXML tracks.
  • Addressed crash decoding some multi-channel DNG files.
  • Addressed render in place handles for frame based formats.
  • Addressed audio input device preference reset after restart.
  • Addressed GPU memory error for some OpenFX on Windows.
  • Addressed artifacts in Sony XAVC Long GOP MXF renders.
  • Addressed missing Text+ inspector controls in older projects.
  • Addressed anchoring issue with Text+ CLS box extend controls.
  • Addressed issues with CustomTool LUT name controls.
  • Addressed issue with clip EQ pasted Q and frequency attributes.
  • Addressed ACES 2.0 artifacts on Windows and Linux.
  • Addressed network paths with accented characters on macOS 27.
  • Addressed file size estimates for spanned RED clips.
  • Updated Fusion tool and scripting reference developer documents.
  • General performance and stability improvements.

DaVinci Resolve Studio 21.2 adds

New features and improvements

  • ResolveFX False Color support for Gen 5 and Gen 6 color science
  • Improved AI assistant color and Fusion capabilities
  • AI assistants can download extras needed for advanced features
  • AI assistants can export frames or order thumbnails as grid
  • Multiple scripting API improvements

Fixes

  • Addressed loss of OpenFX from MultiMaster trim groups on reload
  • Addressed MainConcept H.265 CRF render crash

What's new in Fusion Studio 21.2

The following features have been added or updated.

  • Addressed control naming issue with custom tool and vertex.
  • Addressed anchoring issue with border extension in Text+ CLS.
  • Addressed issue with tube create tool category.
  • Addressed material viewer crash with software rendering.
  • OGraf inspector now shows up to 35 template properties.
  • Addressed OGraf template loading from network and zipped paths.
  • Addressed OGraf render timeout and memory usage issues.
  • Addressed issue with plastic light height control.
  • Addressed issue changing random seed in Shake.
  • Addressed script issues with AddTool and SetInput functions.
  • Addressed issue reading video files with FFMpeg.
  • General performance and stability improvements.

What's new in Fairlight Live 1.1.1

The following features have been added or updated.

  • Support for Fairlight Live Audio Panel 20.
  • Support for Fairlight Live Audio Panel 40.
  • Improved IO management and reporting.
  • Multiple panel UI improvements.
  • Custom screen mapping support for multi-screen panels.
  • Support for panel screensaver after period of inactivity.
  • Do-to-all/selected support in bus management dialog.
  • Added templates for new Constellation IP switchers.
  • Persistent file selector path in cue player.
  • Updated snapshots to show date and time of creation.
  • Improved bi-directional monitoring settings in patching matrix.
  • Addressed issue with layer setup.
  • Addressed 2110 sender issue in panel utility.

  • Panels now reset all screens to home on project load.
  • Addressed issue with channel selection in the index.

entry.summary: 1 minute read Affinity for iPad: what’s free and what’s missing 2:22 Affinity for iPad is free for individuals and combines sketching, vector, photo, and layout tools in one app. Canva might be in some difficulty and relocating or laying off 22% of its workforce , but there's als
entry.content:
1 minute read
Affinity for iPad: what’s free and what’s missing
2:22

Affinity for iPad is free for individuals and combines sketching, vector, photo, and layout tools in one app.

Canva might be in some difficulty and relocating or laying off 22% of its workforce, but there's also new software to talk about. After being free on Mac and Windows since 2025, Canva's Affinity, an all-in-one app for professional design, photo editing, page layout, and sketching, has arrived on iPad. It's purpose-built for touch and, unlike most of its rivals, is a free download from the App Store.

The main caveat is that a Canva account is required to run it. The core tools are free for individuals, and Affinity's free tier contains a lot of functionality, so you only need to cross the company's palm with silver if you want the AI tools.

The app is built around Sketch, Vector, Pixel, and Layout studios. Sketch Studio includes over 350 editable brushes that respond to Apple Pencil pressure, tilt, and barrel roll. Photo tools cover non-destructive editing, composites, selections, and RAW development. Layout handles documents from short brochures to 500-page books, with print-ready output. The app works offline, and a single .af file holds a whole project and is shared with desktop.

Compatibility

Compatibility can be an Achilles' heel for software in this space, but Affinity seems to have it covered. It opens PSD, AI, INDD, IDML, PDF, SVG, and other formats, and exports to JPEG, PNG, WebP, PDF, SVG, EPUB, and INDD, with direct export to Canva. INDD and IDML imports preserve page structure, text frames, and basic styles, but GREP styles, anchored objects, and tables may need manual adjustment. Illustrator files need PDF compatibility enabled, and appearance stacks, masks, and advanced effects may flatten. Layered PSDs open with masks, groups, and adjustments in most cases, though smart objects and advanced filters may flatten.

Still to come

Canva AI Studio tools such as noise clearing, blur rescue, and background removal need a Canva premium plan. Affinity says content in the app is not used to train AI features.

As it stands, some features from the desktop version are not in the iPad version at launch: Books, Batch, Data Merge, Quick Adjustments, the Info and Scope panels, macro recording, and Astrophotography Studio. Free updates are promised, so hopefully they will arrive soon.

entry.summary: 1 minute read Canon EOS C400, C80, C50 firmware: new features 2:46 Canon's free December firmware adds Multi-Matrix color control to the EOS C400, C80, and C50. The C50 also gains Speedlite flash support. Canon has announced a wide-ranging firmware update for the EOS C400, EOS C8
entry.content:
1 minute read
Canon EOS C400, C80, C50 firmware: new features
2:46

Canon's free December firmware adds Multi-Matrix color control to the EOS C400, C80, and C50. The C50 also gains Speedlite flash support.

Canon has announced a wide-ranging firmware update for the EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50 on November 4, 2026.

Multi-Matrix color control and broadcast tools

The firmware update adds Multi-Matrix support across all three cameras, providing control over image color and saturation across selected color axes. Canon says this allows greater precision when matching multiple cameras and working with LED volumes, and helps cameras fit into existing real-time color workflows.

Supporting broadcast and virtual production environments is a bit of a focus with this update, with new features including improved CV metadata for focus and zoom encoder data, black level adjustment when shooting in Canon Log 2 or Canon Log 3, and image stabilization support for lenses exceeding 1000mm. Audio output in Slow & Fast mode is also supported, with Canon citing productions that move between high-speed sports footage and post-match interviews.

Autofocus and slow-motion 

For professional filmmakers using the EOS C400 and EOS C80, the update extends autofocus support in Slow & Fast mode to additional frame rates between 60p and 120p, including 72p, 75p, 90p, and 96p. This allows users to benefit from Canon's autofocus tracking across a wider range of slow-motion shooting scenarios.

The update also improves on-screen display information, including base ISO and fan indicators.

Speedlite flash support for EOS C50

The firmware update adds support for compatible Canon Speedlite flash accessories on the EOS C50 via the Multi-Function Accessory Shoe. This is aimed at professional photographers and hybrid shooters, including wedding and event creators, who want to capture still images using flash alongside video footage from the same event.

Supported accessories include EL-series and EX-series Speedlites, Macro Lights, and Speedlite Transmitters.

Customization and control

The update introduces additional customization options for RF lens buttons, camera control dials, and assignable buttons across the EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50. Users can assign quick access to more functions, including autofocus, digital tele-converter, sensor mode, and exposure settings.

Availability

The new firmware updates for the EOS C400, EOS C80, and EOS C50 will be available to download free of charge from December 2026 via Canon support.

entry.title: Nikon ZR firmware 2.00: RED color science
entry.summary: 1 minute read Nikon has confirmed that ZR firmware 2.00 is coming soon, with support for Log3G10 gamma when recording in H.265 enabling RED color science. Nikon has confirmed that firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, its first major update for the popular full-frame compact ci
entry.content:
1 minute read

Nikon has confirmed that ZR firmware 2.00 is coming soon, with support for Log3G10 gamma when recording in H.265 enabling RED color science.

Nikon has confirmed that firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, its first major update for the popular full-frame compact cinema camera, will be released “soon.” No date has been given, though in September, when it first announced that it was developing the firmware, Nikon said the update would arrive in 2026.

The update adds support for Log3G10 gamma when recording in the compact H.265 video file format, enabling shooting that incorporates RED color science. Nikon’s September announcement paired Log3G10 with REDWideGamutRGB, but this announcement mentions only the former.

The update also adds a selectable level for [High ISO NR], which Nikon’s September announcement specified as applying to H.265 Log recording. Focus peaking display will be available when recording in R3D NE format, the RAW format developed for Nikon cameras to carry RED color science.

There are two new features not on the list Nikon published in September: more functions can be assigned to the command dials and function buttons, giving single-action access to key settings, and a 3D LUT can be applied to HDMI output.

Open gate recording and a desqueeze display for anamorphic lenses are not part of 2.00. In September, Nikon said it was developing both with the goal of including them in ZR firmware in 2027. The same announcement said RED is updating its RED CONTROL and RED CONTROL PRO apps to support remote control of the ZR, with no date given.

entry.summary: 9 minute read DJI Osmo 360 II review: image quality and price 15:26 The Osmo 360 was DJI’s first foray into the world of panoramic video. But now there’s a new device on the block that aims to solve the drawbacks of the original camera. Is it worth the upgrade? 360 video is certa
entry.content:
9 minute read
DJI Osmo 360 II review: image quality and price
15:26

The Osmo 360 was DJI’s first foray into the world of panoramic video. But now there’s a new device on the block that aims to solve the drawbacks of the original camera. Is it worth the upgrade?

360 video is certainly a big thing right now, with a lot of choice out there at different levels of budget. Insta360 is currently the best known company in the field of 360 ‘action’ cameras. But hot on its heels comes DJI with the Osmo 360 II, an update on last year’s camera that aims to fix some of its shortcomings.

That isn’t to say that DJI’s first 360 camera was bad, not by any stretch. But when both its rivals, Insta360 and GoPro, released 360 cameras with replaceable lenses, it was easy to see which choice would give the clearest peace of mind.

So, let’s take a look at what’s been updated, and whether the Osmo 360 II should be on your shopping list for the upcoming Christmas period.

Osmo 360 II, what’s new?

Externally, the Osmo 360 II doesn’t look visually different from the first camera. In fact, the only real giveaway is the logo print on one side of the body. There are some other design variations, such as the microphone cover with integrated wind protection, and what look like small bolts that could possibly make repair easier, but for the most part it looks very similar to the previous camera.

The main change to the external design is the inclusion of replaceable lenses. One of the main vulnerabilities of a 360 camera is the protruding glass, making them susceptible to damage, so including the ability to replace them was a design priority for the DJI team.

The new lenses on the Osmo 360 II are not just replaceable by owners in the field, but they have also been given a boost to their scratch resistance, making them tougher to break or scratch in the first place.

Square sensor, 8K/60, and a bigger battery

The sensor on the camera is a 1/1.1-inch affair that is capable of recording up to 8K/60 when images from the two lenses are combined. That’s a 10 fps boost over last year’s model. SuperNight mode now also works with 8K/60, allowing for slow motion effects under lower light conditions.

The sensor is square, which means that when the 180-degree circular lens image is projected onto the imaging area, much more of the sensor is used than with a 4:3 chip. This follows on from the Action 6, which also features a square sensor. It's a more efficient use of the battery, since there are fewer redundant pixels being left to draw power without contributing to the image.

If you drop the resolution down to 4K, the camera is now capable of recording up to 240 fps. But that does come with some caveats, which I’ll come to in a bit.

The battery has been boosted in capacity to 2150 mAh, and it is backwards compatible with the older camera, as well as being compatible with DJI's Osmo Action cameras.

There’s a new Spotlight Follow mode, which will lock onto a subject and then automatically pan and tilt to reframe the shot to save manually doing it later. Very useful for vlogging or tracking action subjects.

105 GB of built-in storage also features, alongside the usual SD card slot. It is now possible to record 16K 360 timelapses, and there's a four-mic array built to reduce wind noise.

Those are the headline features, so let’s see how it all works in practice.


The Osmo 360 II features much tougher lenses that are user replaceable

Using the Osmo 360 II

From the perspective of using the Osmo 360 II as an action camera style device, next to the GoPro MAX 2 it's a well formed camera to use on a helmet. It’s not quite as low profile as the MAX 2, but it’s certainly better than the vertical form factor of the Insta360 X6. Although Insta360 has now released a horizontal bracket for the X6, it does have some restrictions, which means that the MAX 2 and Osmo 360 II are the better devices to use for such situations.

For general use the button layout works nicely, but on a helmet the buttons are a little difficult to feel, so I would prefer them to be a bit more identifiable when the camera needs to be operated in such a way. I would also like to see some haptic feedback so that in loud environments I would know what the camera was doing when I can't hear the audio chimes.

All that said, general operation of the camera and interface is very similar to the first Osmo 360, and anyone who is familiar with other DJI devices will be able to find their way around easily.

Reliability has never been an issue with DJI cameras, and it isn’t here either. Battery life on the 360 II is extremely good, while the build quality and well thought out design of the port access doors means that they can’t accidentally be opened in vulnerable environments such as in and around water. The 360 II is rated down to 10 m (33 ft) without a case, and down to 50 m (164 ft) with the addition of a dive housing.

Spotlight Follow mode is a great addition to the camera. The 360 II can also be set to recognize individual people via the Registered Subjects option. Once you go into Spotlight Follow mode the camera will automatically detect the person in shot and then wherever you move the camera they will stay in frame. It’s effectively like having a gimbal camera but without the vulnerability.

The NFC connection also works nicely. Just tap the camera on the NFC point of your phone to open the app and connect to the device in one step.

Audio pickup is good. For the best audio it’s always better to use a dedicated mic system such as DJI’s Mic 3, which will directly connect to the camera. But when that isn’t possible, such as in a watersports environment, the audio pickup still works nicely. For example, it picked up my voice well while surfing on a whitewater river wave in a kayak and it didn't seem hugely affected by being waterlogged, indicating good drainage.

Image quality

When it comes to image setup, there’s the option of using the standard color profile or D-Log M, both in 10-bit color. It’s a shame that full D-Log hasn’t been made available, but D-Log M still gives grading potential. As per all DJI devices, the sharpness (called “Texture” in the menus) and noise reduction can be adjusted to taste.

To reduce the electronic look of images I prefer to dial both the Texture setting and noise reduction to their lowest settings, although there are still some aspects of the image that show artifacting despite reducing them.

Haloing and warping in bright light

One of the most noticeable issues is haloing around objects such as trees against a blue sky in bright light. This has been an issue on most of DJI’s recent cameras, but it’s particularly problematic on the Osmo 360 II. It appears to be a result of the HDR style processing that the camera performs to maximise dynamic range, and it can’t be turned off. It appears whether or not you have Adaptive Tone switched on with the standard color profile or you're using the D-Log M profile.

The only way I have found to reduce its appearance is to dial in a -1 EV exposure compensation when I’m using the camera in bright sunlit conditions. When things become duller or overcast, it’s safe to go back to a 0 EV setting to avoid underexposure.


0 EV in bright light shows significant haloing around the trees and my head against the sky

The image is vastly improved by using a -1 EV exposure compensation setting in bright sunlit conditions

The need to do this could preclude the Osmo 360 II from being an easy-to-use device for beginners or those with less technical knowledge. I’ve been discussing these issues regarding DJI cameras for a while now, and it’s long past time that the problems were addressed. You can see from the still grabs above how noticeable the issue is.

It’s not the only problem I found. At times I have come across a strange warping effect, usually occurring behind foreground objects such as a person viewed from a selfie stick.

It might be tempting to think that it’s a stitching effect. But the problem always occurs well away from any stitch line, so something else is going on. Just as with the haloing issue, it could be something to do with merging frames and some of the built-in AI that a lot of these modern cameras use to help with image processing.


360 cameras are always great for POV!

Whatever the reason, it’s an odd and objectionable problem that needs solving. I do have to be fair to DJI, though. I have noticed similar strange issues on other recent cameras from other manufacturers as well. For example on the Insta360 X6, as I’ve used it more, I've spotted funny effects such as the sky appearing to ‘shift’ in the image independently of any camera movement. It doesn’t happen all the time and most people might not notice it. But once you are aware of the potential for the issue, you can’t unsee it.

These problems are clearly a result of the massive amount of processing being performed on the image, but it shows that maybe the technology still has a way to go before it’s perfected.

All that said, if you get the settings right, the image is highly detailed with good dynamic range. Low-light performance is also very good indeed, particularly in the SuperNight mode.

Slow motion: 240 fps is too noisy to use

Originally I was excited at the prospect of 240 fps 360 footage. The image does take a resolution hit down to 4K, but I thought it would be worth it.

Unfortunately, the results I have seen so far have been disappointing. Even in good light, the shadow areas of the image are incredibly noisy to the point where I cannot foresee being able to use shots created in this mode practically.

I have tried increasing the noise reduction setting, but the results are similar. I’m at a loss to explain why the image is as noisy as it is. Simply having to boost the ISO to account for the frame rate doesn’t seem to explain the effect fully.

Luckily, 8K/60 isn’t affected in the same way, so it is still possible to achieve slow motion in the camera at a high resolution. But, it is a great shame that the ultrahigh slow-motion frame rates on the Osmo 360 II are so afflicted by noise as to be almost unusable.


100% crop of a 240 fps clip. The shadow noise is clearly visible here

Editing the 360 footage

Personally, I’m not a fan of editing on mobile apps, so most of my experience of putting together footage from the Osmo 360 II comes from desktop software.

DJI’s Studio software has come a long way from its first version, and most of the kinks appear to have been worked out. My preferred workflow is to use the Studio software to convert the footage to rectilinear format so that I can do my reframing and keyframing directly within Resolve.

I have previously used GoPro’s reframe plugin for Resolve, but that needs to be used within Fusion for proper operation. Handily, DJI has now produced its own Resolve plugin that can be used directly from the Effects tab and simply dragged onto the clip. Because it doesn’t need Fusion, it’s less processor-intensive and works slightly more smoothly than the GoPro plugin. It will also work with 360 footage from other cameras too, since all it needs is the footage in rectilinear format.

If you’re creating POV footage, you will need to make sure you export from DJI Studio with the Direction Lock option for the clip turned on. This will ensure that the view moves with your head. Unlike Insta360’s software, there’s no option to restore the natural movement. This is an option I like about using the X6, because it allows POV footage to move much more naturally with head movement and restores some of the micro-movements. It’s not a deal-breaker, but it would be something I’d like to see implemented in a future DJI Studio update.

Having said all that, the need to go into separate software to export in rectilinear format for editing is still an added editing step that really shouldn’t be required in 2026. I will celebrate the day when Resolve can handle the 360 files from these cameras natively. There’s not really any excuse anymore, given the prevalence of 360 devices now.

Should you buy the Osmo 360 II?

360 cameras have become noticeably better in recent years. We are now at a point where the reframed footage is approaching that of traditional non-360 action cameras. But the question for a lot of potential purchasers is whether they should get a 360 camera rather than a normal action camera, and whether the Osmo 360 II is a better option than the competition.

In terms of ecosystem, if you already own other DJI cameras, then the Osmo 360 II will slot in very well. It’ll have matching imagery and a familiar interface.

For other types of user, I would always recommend a traditional camera as a main go-to device before you invest in a 360 model. The need to do extra processing and editing with 360 footage means that I still regard them as specialist-use devices rather than something you reach for on an everyday basis.

But if 360 is the way you want to go, all of the current 360 models on the market right now have their quirks. If you want to use the camera on a helmet for POV and other adventure use, then the Osmo 360 II and Max 2 would be a slightly better fit than the X6.

However, if you need low-light performance and battery life, then the decision will come down to a choice between the Osmo 360 II and the Insta360 X6. The Osmo is certainly a powerful contender, and if you bear in mind what I said about the EV setting, it can produce some great images.

Price versus the Insta360 X6

Compared to the Insta360 X6, the Osmo 360 II has double the onboard storage and is £110 less expensive at £509 ($571) compared to £619 for the X6. There are other advantages too. The X6 doesn’t allow the use of log recording in its single-lens modes, whereas the Osmo 360 II does. Both cameras do, for some reason, omit the option for 24p in single-lens modes, a design decision that continues to baffle me!

In conclusion, while the Osmo 360 II does have its flaws, it is still a very capable camera that continues to improve upon the 360 devices that came before it. It will fit perfectly within an existing DJI camera ecosystem, and it is also very reasonably priced versus the competition. Just don’t use the slow motion.

entry.summary: 1 minute read GoPro AGV helmet teased: what we know so far 1:51 GoPro has opened a notify-me page for a full-face motorcycle helmet developed with the Italian brand AGV, almost three years after it bought smart helmet specialist Forcite. The first new product announced since GoPr
entry.content:
1 minute read
GoPro AGV helmet teased: what we know so far
1:51

GoPro has opened a notify-me page for a full-face motorcycle helmet developed with the Italian brand AGV, almost three years after it bought smart helmet specialist Forcite.

The first new product announced since GoPro agreed its Starman Optical deal is something it has had cooking for a while. Back in January 2024, when it still felt it had cash to spend, GoPro announced it would acquire Sydney-based Forcite Helmet Systems, maker of the MK1S smart helmet.

It’s taken a while for anything to happen with the acquired tech, but the company has now teased its first helmet, a “fully integrated tech-enabled” design developed with Italian helmet maker AGV. A notify-me page is now live with a short teaser video.

The page gives no specifications, pricing, or release date. GoPro says only that the helmet will give riders “all the tech + performance they need – built-in.” The teaser shows a full-face motorcycle helmet with a camera lens mounted centrally below the visor, and that’s about it. There is no indication of any other tech that may feature, though presumably comms is part of the mix.

The sign-up form suggests this is more than smoke and mirrors, though, inviting people to apply for a Test Pilot Program that asks for a social handle and helmet size from XS to XXL.

At the time of the Forcite acquisition, GoPro said it would both develop its own line of helmets and supply the technology to other helmet brands as an OEM. Only one of those seems to have come to pass, which is probably understandable given the company’s woes. CEO Nicholas Woodman confirmed the AGV partnership on GoPro’s Q1 2025 earnings call, describing a potential $3 billion market for tech-enabled motorcycle helmets.

You just have to hope the lenses are replaceable…

entry.title: Ocarina of Time vs GTA VI: Switch 2 power gap
entry.summary: 2 minute read Ocarina of Time vs GTA VI: Switch 2 power gap 4:16 Nintendo’s remake arrives November 5, two weeks before GTA VI , on a console with under a third of the PS5’s GPU power. Design may still beat specs. Competition between major titles is becoming a theme as we move to
entry.content:
2 minute read
Ocarina of Time vs GTA VI: Switch 2 power gap
4:16

Nintendo’s remake arrives November 5, two weeks before GTA VI, on a console with under a third of the PS5’s GPU power. Design may still beat specs.

Competition between major titles is becoming a theme as we move toward the end of the year. On December 18, two massive films, Dune: Part Three and Avengers: Doomsday, hit movie theaters on the same day, in a move that the industry cannot decide is brave or borderline suicidal. The clash has already been dubbed Dunesday. And this month, two of the biggest video games of the year, Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and Rockstar’s Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI), launch a mere two weeks apart.

 

Beyond the wild difference in content (this is more Barbenheimer than Dunesday), what makes their story particularly interesting is that they launch on hardware at opposite ends of the power scale. And it is the cheaper machine that might be the one making the stronger case for how games should be built in an industry squeezed by rising memory costs and console prices.

We’ve been here before. When Tears of the Kingdom arrived, we looked at how Nintendo turned an underpowered Switch into a platform for one of the biggest releases of all time. Now Ocarina of Time arrives on the Switch 2, which is still underpowered against the machines around it, and that still doesn’t matter.

Switch 2 by the numbers

Nintendo has not published official GPU specs for the Switch 2, but third-party analysis puts it at roughly 3.07 TFLOPS docked and 1.71 handheld, with 12 GB of LPDDR5X memory. By way of comparison, the PS5 offers 10.28 TFLOPS and 16 GB of GDDR6, while the PS5 Pro goes considerably further. In raw GPU terms, the Switch 2 has less than a third of what the base-spec PS5 brings.

That gap matters for a game such as GTA VI, which is built around a vast, dense open world that aims for photorealism. It is hard to imagine it running on Nintendo’s hardware, and Rockstar has unsurprisingly announced nothing of the kind, though it has ported games to Nintendo consoles in the past. (The most recent was Red Dead Redemption on the Switch 2 in December 2025, and Red Dead Redemption 2 is rumored to be on the way, but Rockstar has confirmed nothing.)

Nintendo plays a different game

But Nintendo designs its games around a different set of choices. With the Hyrule of Breath of the Wild and Tears of the Kingdom, it created a huge world and filled it with deliberately stylized graphics that eschewed photorealism for scale and interactivity.

With Ocarina of Time it’s made a different set of choices again. Previews note that Hyrule Field, which keeps the bounded layout of the 1998 original, feels small next to the Breath of the Wild map that Tears of the Kingdom reuses and expands. Whether that is a deliberate trade for polish or simply keeping true to the original, Nintendo hasn’t said (and, of course, the finished product may have a bigger play area). But the remake’s detail is where preview writers seem to be focusing their praise. We should know more soon: Metacritic has pointed to midweek for the review embargo lifting, which could mean Wednesday.

What’s in a frame?

Nintendo has not published a resolution figure for the Ocarina of Time remake, though reports based on its pre-release details list 60 fps. Digital Foundry’s analysis of the September Direct footage found gameplay at native 1080p and 60 fps, with menus at 1440p and no sign of DLSS upscaling (though it did point out some areas where it might actually have helped). That frame rate, though, is about three times that of the N64 original, which ran at roughly 20 fps.

GTA VI will be massive, no doubt about it. But Nintendo seems once more to have pulled off the trick of creating something special on a console that is comparatively feeble next to its rivals. When Tears of the Kingdom came out, we made the argument that you can chase specs as much as you like; it’s the content that really counts. And that is as true today as it was then, not to mention being as appicable to cameras as ever.

entry.content:
1 minute read
Sony LYTIA 720: specs, availability, 4K60 HDR
2:48

Sony's new LYTIA 720 is a 50-megapixel stacked CMOS phone sensor with about 50% less random noise than the LYTIA 700. It supports 4K60 HDR with all-pixel autofocus.

Sony's Semiconductor Solutions Corporation division has announced the LYTIA 720, an approximately 50-effective-megapixel stacked CMOS image sensor for mobile devices. It is a 1/1.56-type sensor with a 10.24 mm (0.40 in) diagonal, 1.0 μm pixels, and a Quad Bayer color filter. Basically, it inherits technologies developed for Sony's LYTIA high-end series and applies them at a lower price point.

Improved low-light performance

Ultra High Conversion Gain (UHCG) circuit technology raises charge-to-voltage conversion efficiency and reduces random noise by approximately 50% compared with the LYTIA 700. In plain English, Sony is claiming better low-light performance.

There are other gains too. Hybrid Frame-HDR (HF-HDR) combines Dual Conversion Gain-HDR (DCG-HDR), which covers low- to medium-brightness ranges in a single exposure, with a short-exposure frame for the high-brightness range. These are then merged in post-processing. Combined with UHCG, HF-HDR gives a dynamic range of 100 dB, though Sony does not say whether that figure holds in video mode. Either way, that takes us very close to 17 stops, 16.6 to be exact.

Optimized AD conversion circuits reduce conversion time and lower sensor power consumption, enabling 4K60 HDR video recording with all-pixel autofocus.

Which phones will get the LYTIA 720?

Sony names no customers and gives no pricing, so there is no confirmed phone yet that will feature the sensor. Mass-production shipping is planned for early November, though, which suggests the first devices will appear in the first half of 2027.

The 1/1.56-type format is common in mid- to upper-mid-range phones, and the LYTIA 700 it replaces has turned up in Motorola, OnePlus, and OPPO handsets. Those brands are the obvious early candidates. But it’s worth pointing out that just because the chip can perform certain tasks, it does by no means mean that the phone it sits in can as well.

We've seen a clutch of Chinese smartphones with impressive camera capabilities in recent months, including the OPPO Find X10 Pro Max and the OnePlus 16. The LYTIA 720 brings those capabilities within reach of mid-price handsets as the main sensor, though you can also expect to see it behind the telephoto camera in higher-price models.
